title: Right Order, Wrong Scale: Auditing LLM Judges for Occupational AI Measurement
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:Right Order, Wrong Scale: Auditing LLM Judges for Occupational AI Measurement
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:LLM judges are increasingly used to assess whether AI outputs meet workplace requirements, but agreement on response rankings does not establish agreement on acceptance rates or occupational aggregates. We introduce O*NET-BENCH, an audit suite derived from an existing survey of 45,796 worker ratings, and evaluate 33 pre-existing judge configurations across six model families on 4,501 test ratings. Twenty-five configurations achieve tie-aware pair accuracy of at least 0.60, although a train-fitted response-only TF-IDF baseline nearly matches the strongest judge. Despite this ordering agreement, judges estimate that 3.0%-97.9% of responses are acceptable, compared with 61.1% for occupation-matched workers. In one fine-tuned lineage, changing from pointwise scoring to a bundled few-shot/listwise protocol improves response ordering while reducing agreement with worker means at the task and occupation levels; this reversal replicates on a task- and worker-disjoint validation split under prespecified criteria. Cross-validated calibration largely removes mean bias, but calibrated scores explain at most 8.5% of individual worker-rating variance. Prediction-assisted estimation yields at most small precision gains at the studied label budgets. These results show that ranking agreement alone is insufficient for occupational measurement. Judges should be validated against the acceptance rates and aggregates their scores will be used to estimate.

report.summary: Auditing LLM judges on occupational tasks finds they often rank responses correctly but misestimate acceptance rates and fail to match worker aggregates, so ranking agreement alone is insufficient.
report.background: LLM-as-judge systems are increasingly used to evaluate whether AI outputs meet workplace requirements, from hiring and task automation to occupational exposure measurement. Many validation pipelines rely on ranking agreement, such as pairwise accuracy or correlation with human preferences, and treat strong rankings as evidence that judge scores can substitute for human ratings. This paper tests that assumption with O*NET-BENCH, an audit suite built from 45,796 worker ratings and 4,501 test ratings, covering 33 judge configurations across six model families. It examines whether ordering agreement translates into accurate acceptance rates and occupational aggregates. The results matter because labor-market studies, policy analyses, and enterprise AI procurement increasingly depend on automated judgments about what work AI can perform.
key_points: O*NET-BENCH audits LLM judges using 45,796 worker ratings, 4,501 held-out test ratings, 33 judge configurations, and six model families. Twenty-five configs reach tie-aware pair accuracy of at least 0.60, but a simple train-fitted response-only TF-IDF baseline nearly matches the strongest judge, questioning whether complex judges add much ranking value.

Ranking agreement hides severe scale errors. Judges estimate that 3.0% to 97.9% of responses are acceptable, while occupation-matched workers accept 61.1%. This means a judge can order responses plausibly yet give wildly wrong absolute acceptance rates, undermining occupational aggregates and downstream estimates of AI suitability.

The paper finds a protocol reversal: in one fine-tuned lineage, switching from pointwise scoring to bundled few-shot/listwise prompting improves response ordering but worsens agreement with worker means at task and occupation levels. This replicating result shows optimization choices can improve one metric while degrading the measurement target.

Calibration helps only so far. Cross-validated calibration largely removes mean bias, but calibrated scores explain at most 8.5% of individual worker-rating variance. Prediction-assisted estimation yields at most small precision gains at studied label budgets, so calibration is not a cure for weak worker-level signal.

The audit concludes judges should be validated against the acceptance rates and occupational aggregates they will estimate, not merely rankings. For occupational AI measurement, tie-aware pair accuracy and leaderboard wins are insufficient evidence that a judge can substitute for worker ratings in policy, procurement, or task-automation decisions.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this challenges LLM-as-judge pipelines that rely on ranking correlation as sufficient validation. Developers should add aggregate-level and acceptance-rate testing, report calibration and uncertainty, and avoid treating judge scores as direct worker proxies. Regular users, including workers, employers, and policymakers, may see occupational AI exposure or task-suitability estimates that appear precise but are not calibrated to human acceptance. The paper argues for auditing judges on the exact population and decision scale they will inform, or combining them with human ratings and explicit uncertainty. It also suggests simpler baselines should be reported before claiming complex judges are necessary.
report.tools: Follow O*NET-BENCH if released, plus the O*NET database for occupational ratings. For judge evaluation, consider HELM, EleutherAI lm-evaluation-harness, OpenAI Evals, Hugging Face Evaluate, and G-Eval or MT-Bench-style protocols. For calibration and analysis, use scikit-learn and statsmodels. When auditing, report tie-aware pair accuracy, acceptance rates, mean bias, and variance explained.
